case_info.scenario: A Black woman in her early 70s with a history of coronary artery disease after coronary artery bypass operations, hypertension, and colon polyps presented to oculoplastic surgery with 1 week of progressive right-sided proptosis and headache, described as severe pain radiating to the back of her head. This was associated with right eyelid ptosis and blurry vision. Prior to presentation, an outside ophthalmologist treated her with 1 week of oral prednisone, 20 mg/d, for presumed orbital inflammation with no improvement. She denied additional symptoms. Notably, she described headache and sudden vision loss in the right eye after coronary artery bypass grafting 1 year ago for several days before spontaneous improvement with incomplete resolution. Personal and family histories were negative for malignant neoplasm and autoimmune disease. Examination revealed right-sided uncorrected Snellen visual acuity of 20/60 associated with restricted supraduction, abduction, and infraduction. Pupils were equal in size without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressures were 10 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Visual fields had temporal restriction to confrontation of the right eye. Vision, motility, and visual fields were normal on the left. Pertinent findings included right-sided proptosis of 2 mm, cranial nerve V1 and V2 hypoesthesia, eyelid ptosis with a margin to reflex distance 1 of 0 mm, optic disc pallor, and vessel attenuation. Outside magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated an infiltrative mass involving right greater than left orbital apices, the right optic nerve, and right extraocular muscles. There was enhancement of the cavernous sinuses, right pterygopalatine fossa, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura (Figure 1).

case_info.caption: Axial (A) and coronal (B) T1 fat-suppressed postcontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrating abnormal enhancing soft tissue with right greater than left involvement of intraconal (yellow-outlined asterisks) and extraconal (white-outlined asterisks) orbital fat and posterior extraocular muscles. The enhancement encases the optic nerves and extends to the cavernous sinus. There is abnormal dural enhancement in the right middle cranial fossa and the right sphenoid wing (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Pertinent findings included right-sided proptosis of 2 mm, cranial nerve V1 and V2 hypoesthesia, eyelid ptosis with a margin to reflex distance 1 of 0 mm, optic disc pallor, and vessel attenuation. [Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no

[Important rules]

* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.
